sections.h2: Can a squatter take ownership of a New York house?
sections.html:
Only by adverse possession, and the statute makes that hard. Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law section 501 says an adverse possessor gains title when the ten-year period in CPLR 212(a) runs out, provided the occupancy was adverse, under a claim of right, open and notorious, continuous, exclusive and actual.

Every one of those elements has to be present for the whole period. An occupant who stays for a few months, who shares the house with the owner, or who pays rent to the owner is not building a title claim under this statute. An owner who sees someone living in a vacant or inherited house should treat it as an urgent problem anyway, because the ten years only start counting while the occupancy continues.

sections.h2: What does a squatter have to prove in New York?
sections.html:
The occupier has to show each statutory element, and the court looks at the facts of the occupancy. The Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law breaks the claim into pieces:

  • Adverse possessor. Someone who occupies another person's real property, with or without knowing about the owner's superior rights, in a way that would give the owner a cause of action for ejectment (section 501(1)).
  • Claim of right. A reasonable basis for believing the property belongs to the occupier. The requirement falls away if the owners cannot be found in the county clerk or register records and located by reasonable means (section 501(3)).
  • Possession without a written instrument. The land must have been occupied through acts open enough to put a reasonably diligent owner on notice, or protected by a substantial enclosure (section 522).
  • Possession under a deed or judgment. Ten years of continued possession under a written conveyance or a court decree, with a separate rule that holding one lot in a divided tract is not holding the others (section 511).

When a claim rests on a written instrument or judgment, section 512 adds a third path: land not enclosed that was used for fuel or fencing timber for farming or the occupant's ordinary needs.

sections.h2: Why does the ten-year period matter to an owner?
sections.html:
The ten years come from CPLR section 212(a), which bars an action to recover real property or its possession unless the plaintiff or a predecessor was seized or possessed of the premises within the previous ten years. A house that sits empty for a long time, often after the owner has died, is where that clock does its damage.

An owner who visits the property, keeps utilities in the owner's name, secures the doors and checks county records for strangers' filings is working against the elements the occupier must prove. The statute does not list those habits, but each one answers the question of whether an owner on reasonable alert would have noticed. Heirs who inherit a house they do not plan to live in should have someone look at it on a regular schedule until it is sold.

sections.h2: How does an owner remove someone who has no right to be there?
sections.html:
Through a court case, not by force. Section 711 of the Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law, found on the Senate's statute page, defines a squatter as a person who enters onto or intrudes upon property without permission and continues to occupy it without title, right or permission. It says a tenant does not include a squatter, and that no tenant or lawful occupant can be removed except through a special proceeding.

Where the squatter rules and section 713(3) conflict, section 713 controls. That section allows a special proceeding after a ten-day notice to quit when someone has intruded on or squatted upon the property without the owner's permission and the occupancy has continued, or permission was revoked and notice given. Section 713 lists other grounds that apply where no landlord-tenant relationship exists:

Grounds for removal where no landlord-tenant relationship exists (source: RPAPL section 713)
SubdivisionSituationNotice
713(3)Squatter, or permission revoked with noticeTen-day notice to quit
713(5)Property sold in foreclosure, deed shown to the occupantTen-day notice to quit
713(7)Licensee whose license expired, was revoked, or whose licensor lost the right to possessTen-day notice to quit
713(8)Former owner who sold to a purchaser for value and stays on without permissionTen-day notice to quit
713(10)Entry or holding by force or unlawful means, where the petitioner was in peaceful possessionNone required

sections.h2: What is the force or unlawful entry route?
sections.html:
Subdivision 10 of section 713 lets the owner proceed without a notice to quit when the occupant entered or remains by force or unlawful means. Two conditions apply: the occupant or a predecessor was not in quiet possession for three years before the forcible or unlawful entry, and the petitioner was peaceably in actual possession when the entry happened, or in constructive possession at the time of an unlawful holding.

That wording means the facts matter a great deal. An owner who left a house vacant and returned to find strangers inside should write down when the house was last occupied by the owner, what locks and fences were in place, and when the occupants were first seen. A New York attorney can say which subdivision fits those facts.

sections.h2: What happens if an owner tries to lock someone out?
sections.html:
A self-help lockout can turn the owner into the defendant. Section 768 makes it unlawful to evict, or try to evict, a person who has lawfully occupied a dwelling for thirty consecutive days or longer, or who holds a lease, except under a warrant or court order. The prohibited conduct includes:

  • using or threatening force to make the occupant leave;
  • cutting off essential services;
  • removing the occupant's belongings or the entrance door;
  • changing or disabling the lock without giving the occupant a key.

An intentional violation is a class A misdemeanor, and each violation can also bring a civil penalty of $1,000 to $10,000. Separately, section 853 lets a person who is put out of property in a forcible or unlawful way recover treble damages from the wrongdoer.

Whether someone is a lawful occupant, a licensee or a squatter can be a contested question. Do not change locks or remove belongings until an attorney has said the proceeding is complete.

sections.h2: How does a squatter issue affect selling a New York house?
sections.html:
An occupant with a claim to the property will show up in the buyer's due diligence and can delay a closing. Tell the title company and the closing attorney about any person living in the house who is not the seller, and ask whether a proceeding under article 7 is needed before delivery of possession.

A seller who has already started a special proceeding should share the status with any buyer, since the court's warrant and the date of possession decide when the house can change hands. If an occupant is a family member, a former tenant or a person the owner once allowed to stay, the right removal ground may be different from the squatter rule, so describe the history accurately.

Owners of a vacant inherited house can also look at probate. Letters from the Surrogate's Court give a fiduciary the authority to manage the property and, unless the will or court says otherwise, to sell it. Our New York probate guide covers that process.

faqs.q: How many years does adverse possession take in New York?
faqs.a: Ten years. Section 501 ties title to the expiration of the CPLR 212(a) limitations period, and the occupancy must have been adverse, under claim of right, open and notorious, continuous, exclusive and actual throughout. Missing any element defeats the claim.

faqs.q: Can I just change the locks on a squatter?
faqs.a: Not safely. Section 768 makes it a class A misdemeanor to evict or try to evict an occupant of thirty consecutive days or longer without a court order, and changing a lock without giving the occupant a key is listed as prohibited conduct. Whether the person is a squatter is a legal question for a court.

faqs.q: What notice does a New York owner give a squatter?
faqs.a: A ten-day notice to quit under section 713, served as section 735 requires, before a special proceeding for someone who intruded without permission. Where the occupant entered by force or unlawful means, subdivision 10 says no notice to quit is required. A lawyer should choose the ground.

faqs.q: Does paying property tax give a squatter title in New York?
faqs.a: The sections reviewed here do not list tax payment among the elements. Title depends on ten years of adverse, open, continuous, exclusive and actual occupancy under a claim of right, or the written instrument and judgment rules. Ask an attorney how tax payments might be used on your facts.

faqs.q: Can a squatter be a tenant under New York law?
faqs.a: No. Section 711 says a tenant does not include a squatter, and defines a squatter as someone who enters without permission and stays without title, right or permission. Someone who has permission, such as a licensee or tenant, is handled under different grounds.
